questions.question: What is a population in a statistical study?
choices: Only those who respond to a survey
Only the largest subgroup
The entire group about which conclusions are sought
Only the observations discarded from the study

questions.question: What is a sample in statistics?
choices: The final conclusion of a study
A subset of the population used to collect data
The entire population in every case
Only the average of the data

questions.question: What is a statistic?
choices: A numerical summary of an entire population only
A survey question
A graph's title
A numerical summary computed from sample data

questions.question: What is a parameter?
choices: A numerical characteristic of a population
Only a sample's mean
An individual survey answer
A random selection method

questions.question: What is a simple random sample of a fixed size?
choices: A sample selected so every possible group of that size has equal chance
A sample selected only from volunteers
A sample chosen from the nearest people
A sample chosen only from one favored subgroup

questions.question: Which method randomly selects students within each grade level before combining the selections?
choices: Convenience sampling
A voluntary response poll
Stratified random sampling
A census of all students

questions.question: What is statistical inference?
choices: Listing every number without interpretation
Using sample evidence to draw conclusions about a population
Guaranteeing each sample equals the population exactly
Replacing data with a personal prediction

questions.question: Why might a voluntary online poll have selection bias?
choices: Every volunteer must answer dishonestly
Online polls cannot contain numerical data
A large response count guarantees a random sample
People choosing to respond may differ from the target population

questions.question: Why does a larger well-designed random sample generally help?
choices: It eliminates every kind of bias
It reduces typical sampling variability
It guarantees an exact population value
It makes random selection unnecessary

questions.question: What is nonresponse bias?
choices: Bias when nonrespondents differ relevantly from respondents
Variation caused only by rounding
An error from counting the same value twice
The natural spread of individual measurements

questions.question: Why should a sample represent important groups in the population?
choices: Every subgroup must have identical opinions
Representativeness requires equal answers
Otherwise conclusions may overrepresent some groups
Only the largest subgroup matters

questions.question: A survey asks only basketball players about all students' preferred sports. What is the main concern?
choices: The survey has too many possible answers
The population cannot be defined
Sport preferences cannot be recorded
The sample favors one subgroup

questions.question: Why does random assignment help in a controlled experiment?
choices: It tends to balance other influences across treatment groups
It guarantees all participants are identical
It ensures the treatment has an effect
It replaces the need for a comparison group

questions.question: Why does an observational association alone not establish causation?
choices: Association means the variables never relate
Causation can never be investigated
Only the sample size determines causation
Other variables may help explain the association

questions.question: What does sampling variability mean?
choices: A population must change whenever it is sampled
Different random samples can produce different statistics
All sampling methods are equally biased
Each respondent changes every previous response

questions.question: A random sample of 100 students includes 40 who use the bus. What population proportion estimate does this give?
A school surveys only students in advanced math classes about all students' homework time. What improves the sampling design?
choices: Survey more students only in the same advanced classes
Select only the students with the highest grades
Use only students who volunteer extra work
Randomly sample across the full student population

questions.question: Two random samples estimate a proportion at 48% and 52%. What is a reasonable interpretation?
choices: One sample must contain deliberately false data
The population necessarily changed by four percentage points
Sampling variability can produce different estimates
Random samples always give identical estimates

questions.question: A researcher randomly assigns participants to tutoring and comparison groups. What distinguishes this from merely observing existing groups?
choices: The researcher assigns the treatment rather than only recording it
The study cannot include numerical data
The assigned groups must have equal final results
A comparison group becomes unnecessary

questions.question: A large convenience sample consistently excludes absent students. What limitation remains?
choices: Its size guarantees complete representativeness
Its size does not remove the coverage bias
Only small samples can be biased
Absent students automatically have the same responses
